{{Short description|Mathematical object}}
{{Technical|date=October 2009}}
In [[mathematics]], specifically [[commutative algebra]], a '''divided power structure''' is a way of introducing items with similar properties as expressions of the form <math>x^n / n!</math> have, also when it is not possible to actually divide by <math>n!</math>.  Just like there are polynomial algebras on n generators, there the foundational object in this setting is the divided power algebra on n generators.

== Definition of a free divided power algebra on n generators ==

Let <math>R</math> be a ring. The free divided power algebra on one generator over <math>R</math>
is <math>R\langle x\rangle</math> and it is supposed to be defined as
<math>R\bigl[\tfrac{x^i}{i!}\bigr]_i</math>.
Lets find a way of defining this without using division because division may not make sense in the ring <math>R</math>.
Define <math>\tfrac{x^i}{i!}:=\gamma_i</math>. Then

<math>
\gamma_i\gamma_j
=\frac{\gamma_1^{i+j}}{i!j!}
=\frac{(i+j)!}{i!j!}\gamma_{i+j}
=\binom{i+j}{i}\gamma_{i+j}.
</math>

This means we can properly define <math>R\bigl[\tfrac{x^i}{i!}\bigr]_i</math> to be

<math>
R[\gamma_i]/\left(\gamma_i\gamma_j=\binom{i+j}{i}\gamma_{i+j}\right).
</math>

Thus this will be our definition of the divided power algebra <math>R\langle x\rangle</math>.
We define <math>R\langle x_1,\ldots,x_n\rangle</math> to be <math>\otimes_i R\langle x_i\rangle</math>
and we call this the free divided power algebra on <math>n</math> generators over <math>R</math>.

== Definition of a divided power structure ==
The preceding section has the following generalization.  Let ''A'' be a [[commutative ring]] with an [[Ideal (ring theory)|ideal]] ''I''. A '''divided power structure''' (or '''PD-structure''', after the French ''puissances divisées'') on ''I'' is a collection of maps <math>\gamma_n : I \to A</math> for ''n'' = 0, 1, 2, ... such that:

#<math>\gamma_0(x) = 1</math> and <math>\gamma_1(x) = x</math> for <math>x \in I</math>, while <math>\gamma_n(x) \in I</math> for ''n'' > 0.
#<math>\gamma_n(x +  y) = \sum_{i=0}^n \gamma_{n-i}(x) \gamma_i(y)</math> for <math>x, y \in I</math>.
#<math>\gamma_n(\lambda x) = \lambda^n \gamma_n(x)</math> for <math>\lambda \in A, x \in I</math>.
#<math>\gamma_m(x) \gamma_n(x) = ((m, n)) \gamma_{m+n}(x)</math> for <math>x \in I</math>, where <math>((m, n)) = \frac{(m+n)!}{m! n!}</math> is an [[integer]].
#<math>\gamma_n(\gamma_m(x)) = C_{n, m} \gamma_{mn}(x)</math> for <math>x \in I</math> and <math>m > 0</math>, where <math>C_{n, m} = \frac{(mn)!}{(m!)^n n!}</math> is an integer.

For convenience of notation, <math>\gamma_n(x)</math> is often written as <math>x^{[n]}</math> when it is clear what divided power structure is meant.

The term ''divided power ideal'' refers to an ideal with a given divided power structure, and ''divided power ring'' refers to a ring with a given ideal with divided power structure.

Homomorphisms of divided power algebras are ring homomorphisms that respect the divided power structure on its source and target.

== Examples ==

* ''The free divided power algebra over'' <math>\Z</math> ''on one generator:''
::<math>\Z\langle x\rangle := \Z\left[x,\tfrac{x^2}{2},\ldots,\tfrac{x^n}{n!},\ldots\right]\subset \Q[x].</math>

: One may see this as a divided power structure also by letting <math>A=\Z[x]</math>, <math>I</math> the ideal generated by <math>x</math>, and the map <math>\gamma_i</math> be defined by <math>\gamma_i(x)=\tfrac{x}{i!}</math>.

* If ''A'' is an algebra over <math>\Q</math>, then every ideal ''I'' has a unique divided power structure where <math>\gamma_n(x)=\tfrac{1}{n!}\cdot x^n.</math><ref>The uniqueness follows from the easily verified fact that in general, <math>x^n=n!\gamma_n(x)</math>.</ref> Indeed, this is the example which motivates the definition in the first place.

* If ''M'' is an ''A''-module, let <math>S^\bullet M</math> denote the [[symmetric algebra]] of ''M'' over ''A''. Then its dual <math>(S^\bullet M)^\vee=\operatorname{Hom}_A(S^\bullet M, A)</math> has a canonical structure of divided power ring. In fact, it is canonically isomorphic to a natural [[Complete space|completion]] of <math>\Gamma_A(\check{M})</math> (see below) if ''M'' has finite rank.

==Constructions==

If ''A'' is any ring then we have the free divided power algebra on ''n'' generators

:<math>A \langle x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n \rangle</math>

defined in the first section above.  Concretely it consists of so called ''divided power polynomials'' in the variables

:<math>x_1, x_2, \ldots, x_n,</math>, 

that is sums of ''divided power monomials'' of the form

:<math>c x_1^{[i_1]} x_2^{[i_2]} \cdots x_n^{[i_n]}</math>

with <math>c \in A</math>. The structure of a divided power algebra(of the third section) is given by letting ''I'' be the ideal of divided power polynomials with no constant coefficient.

More generally, if ''M'' is an ''A''-module, there is a [[universal construction|free]] divided ''A''-algebra on ''M'', called

:<math>\Gamma_A(M),</math>

with PD ideal

:<math>\Gamma_+(M)</math>

and an ''A''-[[linear map]]

:<math>M \to \Gamma_+(M).</math>

(The case of divided power polynomials is the special case in which ''M'' is a [[free module]] over ''A'' of finite rank.)

If ''I'' is any ideal of a ring ''A'', there is a [[universal construction]] which extends ''A'' with divided powers of elements of ''I'' to get a '''divided power envelope''' of ''I'' in ''A''.

== Applications ==

The concrete divided power algebras of the first two sections are ubiquitous in [[algebraic topology]] since a free divided power algebra on n generators is just the dual of a polynomial algebra.  The divided power envelope is a fundamental tool in the theory of [[PD differential operators]] and [[crystalline cohomology]], where it is used to overcome technical difficulties which arise in positive [[Characteristic (algebra)|characteristic]].

The divided power [[functor]] is used in the construction of co-Schur functors.
